title: Okehazama, 2,000 vs 25,000: Who Added Oda Nobunaga's Surprise Detour?
description:
Late on the night of the 18th day of the 5th month of Eiroku 3 (1560), the Imagawa army had already marched into Owari. Yet in Kiyosu Castle, 27-year-old Oda Nobunaga said not a word about how to fight; he chatted until midnight and then sent his retainers to bed.

Following the Shinchō Kōki, this episode walks with Nobunaga through that day: Atsumori at dawn, the dash out of the castle with only five riders, the elders grabbing his horse's bit, his speech on the way to Nakajima fort, a rain like hail that struck only the Imagawa army in the face, and the charge once the sky cleared. "Circling behind the hill for a surprise attack" and "drinking to victory in camp" come from Oze Hoan's Shinchōki, written fifty or sixty years after the battle. The Army General Staff's Nihon Senshi: Okehazama of Meiji 32 also has the detour, and the place name "Dengaku-hazama" and the monks offering sake first appear in that book. Since 1982, researchers working from the Shinchō Kōki have argued there was no detour raid; most researchers today reject the detour theory, but exactly how he reached Yoshimoto is still debated. Last comes Yoshimoto's sword with its gold inlay, and why its signature, "Owari-no-kami", doesn't match "Kazusa-no-suke".

The Shinchō Kōki is quoted from the Meiji-era printed edition on Wikisource; Hoan's Shinchōki from the Genna 8 (1622) old movable-type edition, and the General Staff's Nihon Senshi: Okehazama from the Meiji 32 (1899) edition, both in the National Diet Library Digital Collections. The sword's inscription and the battlefield sites follow the Agency for Cultural Affairs' database of nationally designated cultural properties.

The source of every quotation, year and number is listed in the references below. Old-calendar dates are not converted, and sentences beginning "We think" are this channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone; modern researchers are not drawn.

n001.text: You've heard of this Nobunaga battle: 2,000 beat 25,000 with a surprise raid from behind a hill.

n002.text: But the earliest record of that day differs from your version by one road.

n003.text: Late on the 18th day of the 5th month, Eiroku 3: Kiyosu Castle. The Imagawa army was in Owari.

n004.text: His men waited for their 27-year-old lord's battle plan.

n005.text: No battle talk. He chatted till midnight, then said: go to bed.

n006.text: Leaving, an elder scoffed: luck gone, his mirror of wisdom's clouded.

n007.text: Odder still: next day, rain like hail struck only one side in the face.

n008.text: Over 300 years later, Japan's Army General Staff drew a map of this battle.

n009.text: This file follows the earliest record: under 2,000 men, from midnight to nightfall.

n010.text: That day, which road did he really take?

n011.text: Remember "go to bed"? Before dawn, news came from the front.

n012.text: Two border forts were under Imagawa siege.

n013.text: In his place, army at the gates, front ablaze: what do you do first?

n014.text: He stood up and danced a piece called Atsumori.

n015.text: It goes: fifty years in the human world, set against the heavens, are but a dream; having lived once, what does not perish?

n016.text: Then he cried: Sound the conch! My armor!

n017.text: He armored up, ate standing, put on his helmet and galloped out.

n018.text: Only five mounted pages rode with him.

n019.text: He left before his army had even gathered.

n020.text: Why no battle talk that night? The earliest detailed record is silent.

n021.text: Another copy adds: the elders urged holding the castle; he declined. I guess he'd decided already, and kept quiet.

n022.text: He rode over 10 km southeast in one go. Heading where?

n023.text: Around 7 or 8 a.m. he reached Atsuta; looking east, he saw smoke over the two forts.

n024.text: By then, only about 200 foot soldiers had caught up.

n025.text: At the front-line Zenshōji fort, he gathered arrivals and read the field.

n026.text: Those two numbers from the start? The earliest record is starker: Imagawa, 45,000; his side, under 2,000.

n027.text: 25,000 is an estimate made over 300 years later; some think it's still too high.

n028.text: Even by the low count, that's over ten to one. Would you wait in the fort?

n029.text: The men up front moved first: seeing Nobunaga reach Zenshōji, 300 of them rushed at Yoshimoto.

n030.text: They were soon scattered; both leaders died there.

n031.text: On the hill, Yoshimoto won again.

n032.text: He said: not even demons or gods can stop my spearhead.

n033.text: Taking two forts that morning, he had three utai sung; now, unhurried, they sang again.

n034.text: Utai are the chants sung in Noh. Two wins in a row? I'd probably do the same.

n035.text: Nobunaga saw it too. Instead of staying at Zenshōji, he set out for Nakajima, the frontmost fort.

n036.text: The elders lunged for his bridle.

n037.text: They said: deep paddies on both sides; we'd have to go single file.

n038.text: The enemy will see how few we are.

n039.text: Think: they can count your men at a glance. Would Nobunaga stop?

n040.text: Deaf to them, he shook free and rode on.

n041.text: The version most know: Nobunaga slipped behind the hill to strike from the rear.

n042.text: But the earliest record puts him on this road, in plain enemy view.

n043.text: The first time, I thought I'd misread it.

n044.text: Outnumbered like that, how do you fight?

n045.text: At Nakajima he meant to go on; the elders held him fast.

n047.text: Listen: those men hauled food into Ōdaka Castle last night, then fought at the forts at dawn: up all night.

n049.text: Small army, fear no great foe; fortune lies with heaven. Ever heard that?

n050.text: Yield to a charge; chase a retreat.

n051.text: Take no heads. Cut them down, keep going.

n052.text: Honestly, this speech gives me goosebumps every time. Not one word in it about any detour.

n053.text: Then he led them to the foot of the hill.

n054.text: Later books say Yoshimoto was then toasting victory in camp.

n055.text: The earliest record: he was resting his army on Mount Okehazama.

n056.text: Yoshimoto didn't see the weather turning.

n057.text: And turn it did. 5th month, old calendar: rainy season.

n058.text: Suddenly a squall pelted down like thrown stones and ice.

n060.text: It hit the Imagawa army in the face.

n061.text: The Oda got it from behind.

n062.text: Picture it: your face is dry, and the men opposite face the rain.

n063.text: Stranger still, a camphor tree two or three men could barely hug fell east in the rain.

n064.text: Men said: could this be a divine army sent by the god of Atsuta?

n065.text: Yoshimoto said no demon or god could stop him.

n066.text: What stopped him first was the rain.

n067.text: The rain stopped; the sky cleared.

n068.text: Nobunaga grabbed a spear and yelled: Go! Go!

n069.text: Raising dust like black smoke, the Oda army charged.

n070.text: The Imagawa army scattered back like splashed water.

n071.text: They even abandoned Yoshimoto's lacquered palanquin.

n072.text: Tales say Yoshimoto was too fat to ride, hence the palanquin.

n073.text: In fact, as Ashikaga kin, the Imagawa rode it by special grant. I had to look it up.

n074.text: Nobunaga pointed ahead: the main camp is there! Charge!

n075.text: 300 riders first ringed him in retreat.

n076.text: Clash after clash, only 50 riders were left.

n077.text: First to fight Yoshimoto: Hattori Koheita.

n078.text: In the end, Imagawa Yoshimoto, 42, died at the hands of Mōri Shinsuke.

n079.text: One more detail in the earliest record: the sword Yoshimoto always wore, Nobunaga took and wore himself. Remember it.

n080.text: Before dark, Nobunaga was back at Kiyosu Castle.

n081.text: So where did that road behind the hill come from?

n082.text: That road came from a man a generation after Nobunaga.

n083.text: Earlier, Ōta Gyūichi had recorded this day, in a book called the Shinchō Kōki.

n084.text: Gyūichi fought too: as an archer, the book says, he shot alone from a roof; Nobunaga sent praise three times.

n085.text: Later he served Nobunaga as a clerk. So which road did he write down?

n086.text: Remember the road the enemy could see? That's the one he wrote down.

n087.text: But the book stayed in handwritten copies; the Shinchō Kōki you read today was first printed in the Meiji era.

n088.text: Fifty or sixty years after the battle, a man named Oze Hoan rewrote Nobunaga's story.

n089.text: His book reads like a novel, with many scenes the original lacks. So what did he add?

n090.text: Circle to the hill behind the enemy, furl the flags, creep in: that road first appears in this book.

n091.text: He wrote the drinking party too, plus the retainer with a plan and the Atsuta Shrine prayer; none are in the Kōki.

n092.text: Even the numbers differ: he writes Imagawa 45,000 horsemen, Nobunaga 3,000.

n093.text: Gyūichi went unprinted; Hoan was printed early, edition after edition in the Kan'ei era.

n094.text: In Edo times, most readers met Okehazama through this book.

n095.text: But how did a novel-like book become the answer everyone believed?

n096.text: Remember the General Staff's map from the start?

n097.text: In Meiji 32, the General Staff issued Nihon Senshi: Okehazama, for students of tactics.

n098.text: This book, too, takes Hoan's road: leave some men with extra flags to pin the enemy,

n099.text: while he secretly leads a unit the long way, hidden by the hills, to Yoshimoto's main camp.

n100.text: It even took in scenes only Hoan wrote: the scout's report, armor rattling in Atsuta Shrine, that feast.

n101.text: Surprisingly, the book's own appendix says the Atsuta prayer was probably Hoan's invention.

n102.text: That's strange: the editors clearly doubted Hoan, yet their map still drew his road.

n103.text: The hollow called Dengaku-hazama? This book added it too; it's in neither the Kōki nor Hoan.

n104.text: Local priests and monks with sake and food, the Imagawa off guard: also here.

n105.text: That 25,000 was this book's estimate; it also put Nobunaga's force at Zenshōji at 3,000.

n106.text: When did the standard answer start to crack?

n107.text: After the army's book, this road stayed the standard for 80-plus years.

n108.text: Only in 1982 did a researcher closely reread the Shinchō Kōki

n109.text: and argue there was no detour raid at all. On what grounds?

n110.text: Frontal-attack backers noticed: those weary men Nobunaga spoke of, the Kōki says, rested at Ōdaka Castle after the fight.

n111.text: So the men in front of him were probably not those troops.

n112.text: Later studies also estimate the Imagawa were spread out; Yoshimoto's own camp wasn't that big.

n113.text: Most researchers today reject the detour theory, but exactly how he reached Yoshimoto is still debated.

n114.text: Debate aside, one thing isn't in question: it still exists today.

n115.text: That sword Nobunaga took and wore from then on now rests in a shrine, an Important Cultural Property.

n116.text: On the tang, inside the hilt, a line is inlaid in gold, signed Oda Owari-no-kami Nobunaga.

n118.text: But a researcher notes that in that year he called himself Kazusa-no-suke, not yet Owari-no-kami;

n119.text: the Shinchō Kōki, too, calls him Kazusa-no-suke here.

n120.text: The Agency for Cultural Affairs says it was inlaid when Nobunaga got the sword. But the title doesn't fit: was this line added later too?

n121.text: The records don't say. Same with the place: look for Okehazama today. How many will you find?

n122.text: Two. Toyoake's has been a historic site since 1937; a park in Nagoya's Midori Ward has statues of the two men.

n123.text: We think the detour raid sounds good because it gives the few beating the many a clever reason.

n124.text: So, this file: the detour page isn't in the earliest record; later books added it.

n125.text: How he actually reached Yoshimoto that day: still open.

n126.text: First met Okehazama in a taiga drama, game or textbook? Tell me below.

n127.text: This channel tells only what's in the records. Subscribe to open files with us.
